title: Iran's Ghalibaf Warns 'If We Don't Sell Oil, No One Will' as Strait Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Iran's top negotiator signals Tehran could expand disruptions to all Gulf oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked and Houthi proxies target Saudi shipping routes.
body:
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf issued a stark ultimatum on Wednesday, warning that unless Tehran is allowed to participate in regional oil trade, no country will be able to sell oil — a threat that underscores the deepening energy crisis triggered by the US-Iran conflict.

Posting on X, Ghalibaf declared that the security of the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20 percent of global energy supplies have historically flowed — depends on the absence of American forces. He encapsulated Iran's position in three words: "either all or none."

The 'Either All or None' Doctrine

Ghalibaf's statement represents the clearest articulation of Iran's strategy in the current conflict: if Tehran cannot export its own crude, it will ensure no Gulf state can either. The warning extends beyond the Strait of Hormuz itself, implicitly threatening the alternative export infrastructure that Saudi Arabia and the UAE have relied upon since the waterway was largely blocked following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28.

Maritime risk assessment firm MARISKS characterized Iran's posture as "perhaps the most significant development" in the current crisis. Pointing to Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline and the UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline — both designed to bypass the Strait of Hormuz — analysts warned that Iran's willingness to target alternative infrastructure means there is no simple workaround for Gulf exporters.

"Iran's message is equally clear: Either all regional energy producers can export, or no one does."

— MARISKS, maritime risk assessment

Houthis Open a Second Front

Ghalibaf's warning came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen escalated the conflict by declaring a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. The move threatens to choke off Saudi Arabia's primary alternative export route, which had been handling roughly 5 million barrels per day from the kingdom's Red Sea port of Yanbu.

Two tankers carrying a combined 2.7 million barrels of Saudi crude bound for China and India — the Xin Long Yang and the Rodos — made U-turns on Tuesday, diverting toward the Suez Canal rather than risk passage through the Houthi-controlled strait, according to shipping data on LSEG.

British maritime security firm Ambrey warned that vessels calling at Saudi Arabian ports were "at high risk" and advised shippers to reconsider Red Sea transits.

Oil Markets Under Pressure

The twin disruptions have sent crude prices sharply higher. Brent futures have surged more than $20 per barrel this month, briefly touching $95 on Wednesday — the highest level since early June. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained 2.3 percent to $85.15. Brent has been in technically overbought territory for seven consecutive sessions, the longest such stretch since June 2025.

US gasoline prices have climbed back above $4 a gallon. The crisis has been compounded by the logistical challenges of rerouting oil around both blockaded chokepoints. The largest crude carriers cannot transit the Suez Canal fully laden, forcing shippers to unload cargo south of the canal and reload near Alexandria before circumnavigating Africa — a process that adds weeks and costs to deliveries.

Analysts at SEB Research acknowledged a slim possibility that the latest American strikes could strengthen Washington's negotiating position before a compromise reopens Hormuz. "However, the risk is a more prolonged stalemate, with continued uncertain energy flows, higher oil prices and recurring attacks," they cautioned.

India's Energy Equation

The crisis has direct implications for India, one of the world's largest oil importers and a major buyer of Gulf crude. Indian oil imports from the Middle East have already plunged 27 percent since the Hormuz crisis began, forcing refiners to increase purchases from Russia and other non-Gulf sources. But the closure of the Red Sea route threatens to disrupt those alternatives as well, since some Russian crude reaches Indian ports via the same shipping lanes.

India's refining sector — the world's fourth-largest — depends on reliable crude supply to keep domestic fuel prices stable. Prolonged disruption to both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb could force the government to draw down strategic petroleum reserves or accept higher import costs that feed through to consumer prices.

What to Watch

The conflict shows no signs of abating. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told senators that the war has cost $37.5 billion so far and asked Congress to approve another $70 billion in supplemental funds to replenish depleted missile supplies. Trump has renewed threats to strike Iran's nuclear facilities at Natanz. Iran's health ministry reported 50 civilians killed and 500 wounded in recent US strikes.

Ghalibaf's ultimatum signals that Iran's negotiating position is hardening, not softening. For oil markets and energy-importing nations including India, the message is clear: there is no quick exit from this crisis.
